The inclusion of “pacification” among the items of special work must be reckoned a new departure. This decision, though set in motion from the Center, was carried out in the regions of rebellion-suppression; yet between the Center and the localities there was never any thorough communication, so that in not a few regions the military and political chiefs neither knew of it nor understood it, or still, with old eyes, saw in it no more than “political work” under a fresh face. For this reason it could not produce the effect looked for. What is now called “field-service administration” and “political warfare” both bear upon “pacification work,” and might well be studied together. The “pacification unit” is no combat unit: it can neither fight a positional battle nor sustain one of attack and defense; its greatest use is to render service to the organs to which it is attached, meeting their needs by the four capacities it possesses. And attachment is never so direct or so close as subordination; henceforth, should pacification work still have a value of its own, there would be no harm in considering its incorporation into strategic dispositions and its being set upon a regular footing.

The “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps” was at first attached to the “Beiping Field Headquarters,” and afterward attached to the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters.” The director of the former was Li Zongren, the commander-in-chief of the latter Fu Zuoyi, and these two men each harbored his own designs; in the relation of attachment, it was not merely that they were not “glued” together—they did not so much as come near to being “stuck on.” Placed in such a case, one who wished to expand the work could rely on nothing but self-starting and volunteering.

This chapter sets down a single story which may look somewhat like great thunder and small rain, top-heavy and thin at the foot; yet it is, for all that, orderly and measured, whole from head to tail. Proceeding from historical origins, working through the techniques of the work, and bearing a weighty responsibility—all of it was for no other end than to obtain intelligence material.
For this case the First Brigade once received a large sum in prize money bestowed by the Ministry of National Defense, together with a commendation that it had operational value.

In truth “value” is a thing of measure and limit, and vanishes with the passing of time. It is only the tragic endings of several of the chief figures in the whole story that are enough to give a man pause.

To carry forward “pacification work” was a new departure, set in motion at the Center and put into effect in the regions of rebellion-suppression. Though this was a decision of the Center, between the Center and the localities there was never any thorough communication; indeed in not a few regions they had no notion at all of what the thing was.

By this time the military and political authorities of the localities had for the most part already opened their “bandit-suppression” operations, and in a number of regions were in the thick of fierce combat. Among their common demands, some petitioned the Center for a strengthening of forces, some asked the Center for a replenishment of equipment, and some expressly asked that specialist arms (engineers, artillery, and the like) be sent in support; but never was it heard that any one region, or any one combat unit, had asked that a “pacification unit” be sent to lend its aid. Of course, no quarter knew that a special-operations unit of such capacities had already been formed; and beyond that, in idea and in understanding, they had none of them yet grasped or perceived that this was precisely a surprise-force for the smiting of the devil.

Though this force was parceled out to the several regions on the same terms throughout, the effect it produced differed greatly, by reason of differences in the manner of leadership, in the relation of attachment, in the environment of the locality, and in the strength or weakness of the adversary. As to the “manner of leadership,” the subjective factors weigh heaviest there, and we shall let that pass. Take only the “relation of attachment,” and it was of the utmost importance; for if that were ill-managed, then let a man have talent as great as the sky, and he could bring none of it to bear.

Now let me first explain what the “relation of attachment” is. “Attachment” differs from “subordination”: “subordination” is like the direct line of descent, while “attachment” is as it were a collateral branch. This distinction of near and far, close and distant—say nothing of forty years ago—holds good even to this day: the closer the bond, the easier the business goes. That is to say, when the pairing is apt, one shows to advantage the more readily. Let me illustrate by real instances. The “Second Brigade of the Pacification Corps” was parceled out to the Northeast and attached to the “Northeast Bandit-Suppression Headquarters”; its several command rooms were likewise attached, each to a provincial government or a combat force, and because all were of the “Central system” there was basically no rejection, so that it brought great effect to bear and became the most distinguished of the Pacification Corps’ brigades. Take again the “Fifth Brigade of the Pacification Corps,” parceled out to Shanxi; but the military and political authorities of Shanxi had a whole self-satisfied way of their own, and toward the pacification force sent by the Center, though they did not refuse it, they had no mind to receive it either—the threshold was guarded strict beyond all reason, there was simply no way to get in, and what work was there then to be done?
From this one may see how important it was to establish a sound “relation of attachment.”

Writing to this point, the writer must, in grief and without concealment, point out that in that period (from the victory in the War of Resistance down to the whole mainland’s falling to the Communists), though the Communist Party was fomenting disorder everywhere and was already rampant in the extreme, yet on our side there still prevailed “the setting-up of separate doors,” “the covert strife of factions,” and the foolish notions of “each holding his own quarter” and “marking off a patch to keep oneself safe.” Do not be deceived that such men sang loud of unity with their mouths; in their tread they were marching toward division. In the end the rivers and hills changed color, all came to nothing, and every one of us was a loser—too late then for regret. In truth these words are by now a threadbare commonplace; men of around sixty have long known them by heart, and the general run of intellectuals and of those who followed arms or politics have, without exception, this bitter and intimate experience of it. But the younger generation, under fifty, do not necessarily have such an understanding. To have the chance to speak it out and let them know a little of it is likewise a mirror, lest those wretches who cannot tell good from ill, who sit amid blessing and know not their blessing, should still think to run riot, misleading themselves and others, and even bringing harm upon the state and society.
To turn the subject about, let me begin again from the relation of attachment of the “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps.”
By the regulations, the “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps” was attached to the “Beiping Field Headquarters of the Chairman of the National Government.”

The “Beiping Field Headquarters of the Chairman of the National Government,” “Beiping Field Headquarters” for short, was at that time the highest military and political organ of the North China region, Beiping and Tianjin included. The director of the “Beiping Field Headquarters” was Li Zongren, stationed at Beiping; and for its offices, following the usage of former days, it had chosen the “Juren Hall” within Zhongnanhai.

By the procedure, the writer was, in his capacity as brigade commander, to present himself in person with the official documents to report for duty, and only after ratification could he begin operations in the Beiping-Tianjin region.

On the other side, the “Beiping Field Headquarters,” upon receiving the official documents from the Ministry of National Defense, was by its authority to transmit orders to its subordinate units that all alike take note. Only thus could we “get through” in the Beiping-Tianjin region.

Concerning the establishing of the relation of attachment after the parceling-out, the Corps Commander, Mr. Liu Peichu, also touches on it briefly in Fleeting Glimpses of a Floating Life, where he says: “At the time of the parceling-out, neither was any explicit order issued, nor were any documents of proof given; the Ministry of National Defense merely gave to the military and political chiefs of the several quarters, each severally, a secret telegram, requiring that, ahead of our own troops, they begin to practice the concealment of identity, as a kind of exercise for penetrating deep into the bandit areas.” Did the “Beiping Field Headquarters” receive the Ministry of National Defense’s secret telegram? And what did the secret telegram say? Of all this I know nothing; in fact, I went to report for duty carrying an “official document.” And this “official document,” too, had been given me by the Corps Headquarters when I set out from Nanjing. Otherwise, should I not have been left without a shred of “warrant,” and on what ground could it have been proved that I was the brigade commander? So it should be said that, besides the “secret telegram,” there was also an “official letter.”

Corps Commander Liu’s meaning is that the “secret telegram” was used with the main aim of practicing the concealment of identity, so as to penetrate deep into the Communist areas. In truth these are purely two separate matters, and there is no need at all to drag them forcibly together, lest the more one stirs them the muddier they grow.

To my mind, the “concealment of identity” can be practiced only upon an individual, and not upon a body of several hundred men carrying great quantities of equipment, clad in military uniform, and marching in mighty array. Should the work make it necessary to “penetrate deep into the bandit areas,” that too is confined to an individual, or at most to a few, and by no means to a whole unit; plainly it has nothing to do with “secret telegram or explicit writ,” still less any need to take this for a “subject of instruction” to be practiced.

Speaking of “practice” or “exercise,” I cannot but call to mind a small story, which there is no harm in telling for all to hear. When the first term of the “Lizhi Class” was in training, the Leader was once to come and give an address; our Corps Commander, seized by a sudden whim, came running to consult me. His design was to appoint one trainee to play a malefactor, armed and harboring evil intent, whose lurking should be exposed, so that the other students, discovering him, would denounce him by name, the weapon be searched out on the spot, and the case thus be cracked. At the same time he hoped that students of the First Company should each play the two roles, of the right side and the wrong; and there was of course in it the notion of having me “take the thing in hand.” The moment I heard it—how could this do? Were misunderstanding to come of it, I could never bear the blame; and so I resolutely declared my opposition, and urged him to give the notion up, that on no account would it do, whereupon it was dropped. I thought to myself that, meeting with a superior so naive, there was, beyond being caught between tears and laughter, nothing for it but to sigh in vain.
These few idle words said, let me go on to set down the course of the reporting for duty.

From the latter period of the War of Resistance down to the present, the thirty-sixth year of the Republic, the post of chief of the Second Section (in charge of intelligence and public-security affairs) in such military and political organs as the “Chairman’s Field Headquarters,” the “Pacification Office,” the “Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” the “Garrison Headquarters,” and the “Defense Headquarters” was “by usage” recommended by the “Juntong”—a “right” that Mr. Dai Yunong had won in his lifetime, and not a “system.” Though Mr. Dai has now passed away, this “usage” stands as before, unchanged. As I mentioned earlier, the present chief of the Second Section of the “Beiping Field Headquarters” was my friend Zhang Jiaquan, with whom I was well acquainted; earlier still, in the days when I served as chief of the “Tianjin Station,” he was a “directly subordinate section chief” at Cangzhou on the Jin-Pu line. On the matter of reporting for duty I had already sought his counsel by word of mouth, and he had shown me that I need only go to the Field Headquarters and find him when the time came, and that he would arrange all the formalities to be attended to.

The “Beiping Field Headquarters” was set up in the “Juren Hall” within Zhongnanhai. To enter by the main gate, one had to go in from East Chang’an Street; the gate was strictly guarded, a form to be filled out for visitors, questioning upon questioning, a great vexation—in such a place, to wear a military uniform might well have saved a deal of trouble. To go in by the back gate was the more convenient. By now I have forgotten on what street Zhongnanhai’s back gate stood; I remember only that it was a broad and spacious avenue: past “Beihai Park” one had to go up a great bridge, and, coming down from the bridge, on the right hand stood the famous “Beiping Library,” and on the left was Zhongnanhai.

This great bridge, too, has much that is worth the telling. From childhood the writer walked across this bridge on foot, looking now east, now west as he went; and in winter as in summer there was scenery worth the seeing. Grown up, whenever I crossed this bridge seated in a yangche (a rickshaw), I always felt how hard the puller labored; in winter the steam fairly rose from his head. Later, when there were pedicabs, one of small strength could not pedal up it, but had to jump down and, gripping the handlebars, push and pull together to get barely across; for the bridge was arched, and its curve was considerable—that is, the crown of the bridge was rather high, so that a want of strength, or a heavy tonnage of passenger, would of course not do. As for riding in a motorcar, one passed over with a single roar, and yet the bridge bore a great pressure. Was it then so delicate as all that? Just so; and it is precisely here that my many feelings toward this bridge lie. It is a pity that the writer knows little, and has never applied himself to research it, but has only heard others tell of it—and what one hears, moreover, is not necessarily correct; let me nonetheless speak of this bridge by the way. It turns out that this bridge was in fact two bridges, the one named “Jin’ao” and the other “Yudong,” set side by side east and west, each answering to the other. At the very crown of each was built a rich stone memorial archway, bearing above it a tablet inscribed severally with the words “Jin’ao” and “Yudong.” The building-stone of the bridge-body and of the balustrades was of one uniform white marble, finely carved and wrought, of a crystalline jade hue, in aspect most elegant and yet majestic. By “ao” is meant that the arch of the bridge is like the back of the great sea-turtle; by “dong,” the long rainbow—which just describes it as one great white arched bridge of stone.

What is called “Han white jade” is in fact a kind of milk-white stone resembling marble, firm and fine in grain, not only handsome but lasting long without wearing away. This stone must surely have a correct name; “Han white jade” says no more than that it is of noble worth.

This bridge runs east and west, built to span Zhongnanhai and Beihai, and is indeed the dividing line between Zhongnanhai and Beihai. It shows at the same time that Zhongnanhai and Beihai are joined. Besides Zhongnanhai and Beihai, there is linked together with them yet another park called “Shichahai,” which was originally an artificial lake; from what time it was divided into three parts, one cannot say. One source states that as far back as 1179 the Jin dynasty dug out the water and heaped up the hill, building here an artificial lake, which, through the three dynasties of Yuan, Ming, and Qing, was repaired and built upon, and has lasted to this day. As to the dynasty and the year in which the Jin’ao-Yudong Bridge was built, there must likewise be some record in the annals; suppose it were the middle Qing?
That would be about two hundred years or so. This might of course be ranked a monument of the first class.

The bridge was several hundred feet long, its breadth enough for traffic both ways, and its deck too was paved with Han white jade, each slab about a meter by two—a grand conception indeed. From what time it had been opened to vehicles there is no knowing; some several tens of years, no doubt, had it been traveled. When, in the late autumn of the thirty-sixth year of the Republic, I crossed this bridge again, though on the surface no trace of damage could be seen, yet it had not withstood the erosion and wearing of the long years, and the deck had already worn round and bald and shown itself none too even.
What I felt was this: a bridge so stately, so noble, so fair and ancient—why was it not well cherished?

The deepest impression of all was to behold this great bridge again after a heavy rain had washed it clean; that was truly a case of: this sight should belong to Heaven alone—how many times may it be seen in the mortal world?

Now, on the day that I went alone to the “Beiping Field Headquarters” to report for duty, I wore a Zhongshan tunic and rode a pedicab hailed from the street, and once again passed over the Yudong Bridge. Coming down from the bridge and turning left, one reached the Juren Hall of Zhongnanhai; I entered by a great gate that had no guard—this gate too must have had its name, but I had never once taken note of it. The pedicab went forward all along the way, willows drooping low on the one side of the road and a few households on the other—this was plainly the countryside; how could one speak of an inner court of the imperial palace? After another stretch of narrow stone-paved road I came to a certain place, and looking up saw, opened in the great enclosing wall, a corner gate with guards on watch; I handed in my calling card, and in a moment word came out that said, “The section chief begs you enter.” Well then—and with that I walked into a maze of bewilderment, out of which, but for someone to lead me, I fear I could never even have found my way.

This was no more than the office of the Field Headquarters’ Second Section; where exactly the “Juren Hall” was I had no notion at all. When I had met Section Chief Zhang—my friend Jiaquan—I first handed over the official letter I had brought, and he read it once through, bade me sit and wait a little in his office, and went out with the letter in hand.

In a little while my friend Jiaquan came back and said, “The director (Li Zongren) is in a meeting; you will first be received by Chief of Staff Xu—please come with me.” And so we went out by one door and in again by another, turning this way and that, and came to the Chief of Staff’s office. Though it was a single-story building, it was both lofty and large; how lofty and large in the end? That, of course, one cannot say; but by comparison one always felt that those within it had every one become a small figure. From without, one saw only rows upon rows of great tiled houses, marked off into many courtyards, each of its own plan, so that an outsider naturally could not make out which unit was set up in which place. Within, all was offices partitioned off by screen-panels, and though every furnishing was of the choicest sort, in taste they were utterly ill-matched.

Lieutenant General Xu Qiming, the Field Headquarters’ Chief of Staff, received me with courtesy, and I of course had to be all reverence and respect. When he had read the official letter I brought, he endorsed it with two lines in writing-brush, and then handed it to Section Chief Zhang.
Section Chief Zhang, having asked whether there were any further instructions, signaled with his eyes to tell me that I might now withdraw.

Taking my leave of Chief of Staff Xu’s office, my friend Jiaquan showed me the endorsed document, which, it turned out, read: “First: to be noted by the First Section. Second: the Second Section to keep in close liaison.” The formalities of reporting for duty were as simple as that. I asked my friend Jiaquan, “Ought I to come again and see Director Li?” He thought a moment and answered me, “Wait until the briefing; then we can have a private talk.” When my friend Jiaquan saw me out, he asked where my car was parked, and I could only tell him I had come by hired pedicab. He said, “Whichever way you go out, it is a good long stretch; better let my car take you back.” The car went by the front gate, and the places we passed seemed somehow known to me of old; and bowing my head in thought, I found that this, again, was a thing of more than ten years before.

In the twenty-second or twenty-third year of the Republic, in the days when He Jinggong (Yingqin) presided over the “Beiping Branch of the Military Affairs Commission,” he too had his offices in the “Juren Hall” of Zhongnanhai; and at that time the one who, on behalf of the “Special Services Department” (the forerunner of the “Juntong Bureau”), kept up constant liaison with He Jinggong was the special commissioner, Mr. Zheng Jiemin. The writer was then chief of the “Beiping Station” under the special commissioner’s command.

Later, He Jinggong, the situation having changed, returned to Nanjing, and Mr. Huang Fu (Yingbai), in his capacity as chairman of the “Beiping Political Affairs Reorganization Committee of the Executive Yuan,” acted in He Jinggong’s stead, still keeping his offices in the “Juren Hall.” Presently Mr. Zheng Jiemin too was transferred away and went south from Beiping, and the charge of keeping liaison with the highest authorities at Beiping fell in turn to me.

This liaison or communication, so called, was in principle no more than to “be ready for consultation” and to “undertake designated matters.” Yet if some matter were indeed handed down to be dealt with, whether to do it or not was not for me to decide; I still had to seek instruction from my superiors.

I remember that in all I was twice granted an audience by Chairman Huang; he raised no questions, nor did he ever ask us to do anything. Yet he was concerned for the concealment of our identity. Chairman Huang plainly stated that, should there be need, he could arrange an open post for me, the better to facilitate my activities. He put it more concretely: as things then stood, both the “superintendency of the First Inner District of the Beiping Municipal Public Security Bureau” and the “chief of the First Police Section of the Ping-Han Railway” could be contrived to place me, and he hoped I would consider it and give him an answer.

As I understood it, the jurisdiction of the “First Inner District sub-bureau” included the famous Beijing Hotel, the bustling Wangfujing Avenue, and the neighborhood of Dongdan, where foreign residents lived; the “First Police Section of the Ping-Han Railway” ran from Beiping to Zhengzhou. Both these posts looked very good indeed—not only could they conceal my identity, they could also make for the smoother carrying-on of the work—and my heart could not but be moved by them; but I dared not agree to his face, for I first had to report to my superiors and await their ruling.
In the end the decision of my superiors was “on no account whatever.” Why? My superiors would not explain their reasons.

Some years later, when I had grown a little more seasoned, I heard from friends in chat that both these posts were hard to hold: they were fine targets alike for the chasing of the deer and the chasing of the stink—for one who wished to do work, it was easy to show to advantage there, and for one who wished to scrape up a few dollars, they too were his for the taking. Whether it be so or not, I do not know.

On one occasion, at a briefing of the various intelligence and security units of Beiping, I asked my friend Zhang Jiaquan again whether I should go once more to see Director Li of the Field Headquarters. My friend Jiaquan said, “To my mind, if you wish to see him, you may get in touch with me at any time; and if you find it too much trouble and do not go, that too is of no consequence—seeing him or not, it comes to the same thing; in fact, he has no wish to inquire much into our affairs.” That being so, I gave up the notion of an audience with Director Li; for the coordination of the work, to keep in close touch with the Field Headquarters’ Second Section was enough.

Ever since this force—the “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps”—was established at Beiping, many of the writer’s old friends, hearing the news, came to throw in their lot with me. This was no normal thing; it could happen, I think, only in a real environment that had gone off the rails.

This little force of which I was brigade commander, in a time of peace or under normal conditions, amounted to no more than a battalion; its establishment left little elasticity for the employment of men, and could by no means take in all the heroes of the several roads, from the Three Mountains and the Five Peaks. It was thanks only to the several hundred “operational billets” in the force, easy to place men in, that it was got up into a grand show of refusing none who came.

If it be said that they all came together to offer their service because they had no door by which to oppose the Communists, that is not wholly so. As I myself understood it, the greater part were ready to throw in their own selves, and hoped at the same time that “I too am to be among them”; put from another angle, it was a psychological demand that, should there be some achievement in the future, perhaps a share of it might be mine. Still, since our mission was “pacification and the suppression of rebellion,” they would of course follow along without the least hesitation.
As for making use of old connections as a recommendation—this too is the common way of things, and what is there in it to wonder at?

The tone of these last few words may seem a little unbridled, and a man of a more cautious sort might, it may be, feel there was something arrogant in them, and even mistake them for “harboring ambition” or “meaning to rebel.” There is no harm in saying frankly: who does not wish to climb higher and do somewhat more? Yet I would by no means run wild; how much I myself weighed I had long since reckoned up. My aim was nothing other than, under the leadership of a wise and enlightened Leader, to bend all my strength to breaking free of the arbitrary manipulation of those men who set out from personal interest—and is there, then, anything in this that ought not to be? On this question let us stop here; it is not fit to say much more.

In what follows I shall introduce, one by one, the comrades and friends who came from the several places. In the first section of the first part of my humble work, “Rooting Out Traitors in the North,” I mentioned the name of Jiang Tian—telling how, at the house of a kinsman of his, I met the mysterious figure Fan Xing (Ji Man), from whom afterward many stories were drawn out. This time, at Beiping, I met with Jiang Tian again, and, upon our mutual agreement and the ratification of my superiors, he joined this force.

Jiang Tian, styled Lisheng, was a man of Yutian in Hebei, a graduate of the fourth term of the Military Academy. In the spring of the fifteenth year of the Republic we enlisted together in the First Regiment of the Military Academy, he in the Ninth Company and I in the Tenth, both under the same battalion. I still remember that our regimental commander was Guo Darong (of Baoding Officers’), our battalion commander Zhao Jinwen (of the Yunnan Military Academy), his company commander Yu Yong (of the first term of the Military Academy), and mine Ding Weijing (of the Yunnan Military Academy). He passed the advancement examination and was placed in the fourth term; I failed the examination and had my enlistment prolonged, and so was of the fifth term.

What I would specially explain is that my friend Jiang Tian had an uncommon family background. His uncle Jiang Hao, an old Communist, was in those days as renowned as Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, and had died in his early years at Vladivostok. Jiang Hao’s son—that is, Jiang Tian’s elder cousin Jiang Zhenhuan, of the first term of the Military Academy—died at Tianjin in the eighteenth or nineteenth year, on a charge of rebellion. Of Jiang Hao’s three daughters, two and a half were Communists—by “a half” is meant one who hovered between within the door and without. Though my friend Jiang Tian was close to his several cousins, yet he was no Communist, nor did his thinking lean to the left; the reason for which I could not at first make out, and only later came to know: that his sense of life ran clean counter to that whole creed which the Communists set up as their banner.

I knew his abilities were quite good, and had a great mind to invite him into the force; he too showed himself willing to rouse himself, that we might all do a fine piece of work together, and so we struck it off at a clap, and he condescended to the post of commanding officer of the First Brigade. As to how he did? That the sequel will make plain.

Lieutenant Colonel Bai Jiaqi came too, of whom I have made mention in the fourth part of my humble work. We had not known each other before; when I was serving my sentence in “Tilanqiao Prison,” Lieutenant Colonel Bai Jiaqi was a warder over the suspected Japanese war criminals. We were held on the second floor of the Loyalty Ward, and the Japanese prisoners on the third and fourth—which, to tell it, was itself a strange thing. One day he stood outside the iron railing and called to me, introduced himself, and thereupon sent in a rich and abundant fare, seldom to be had, which I might share with my “schoolmates”; and so we came to know each other. Now, since he had come, sparing not a journey of a thousand li, I not only welcomed him with all my heart, but reported the case specially and requested that he be appointed lieutenant colonel and brigade adjutant.

Who came first and who came after, in point of time I can no longer keep straight. There were, again, three men who came together from Shanghai to Beiping. We had perhaps met once or twice, but had had little to do with one another, and so were not very well acquainted. Not long before the victory in the War of Resistance, the puppet “Political Defense Bureau” (the former “Special Operations Headquarters” at No. 76) had taken on three newly-fledged Japanese-language interpreters; though men of Shandong and of Hebei, they had all grown up in the Northeast, and afterward had gone together to study in Japan (at Waseda). Their level of knowledge was rather high, and they were altogether unlike the general run of Japanese interpreters, who were steeped in bad habits. That they became interpreters in a puppet organization was, I suppose, because even they themselves could not tell which was the true and which the false, and it was not necessarily of their own will. These three men were Wang Zhibin, Qi Zhenping, and Guo Zizhong; their coming this time, too, was upon the guidance of my friend Liu Yuanshen. As to how to arrange their work, that cost no little pains; in the end they were formed into a small group, with Wang Zhibin appointed group leader, and sent to Tianjin to devote themselves to the gathering of intelligence. Beyond all expectation, they did not fail the trust, and their harvest was great.

To speak again of my old partner from the former “Shanghai District,” my friend Zhang Zuoxing. He had served in the “Shanghai District” as inspector of the wireless station, and at the end of October in the thirtieth year was arrested about the same time as I. Afterward he was held for a period at “No. 76,” and then lived “in idleness” at “Huacun,” in extreme hardship, having no means of livelihood. After I had shaken off my bonds and could move about—it was about the thirty-second year—I recommended him to the puppet “Chairman of Anhui Province,” Luo Junqiang, who appointed him to a term as magistrate of Fanchang County in Anhui—which was of course a puppet post. Though we had made an arrangement before he set out, we were hampered by the difficulty of communication, and nothing came of it. For this reason I did not mention his whereabouts in the fourth part of my humble work. This time, returning to Beiping, he had already brought his family and settled here; and to keep out of others’ notice, he lived retired and seldom went abroad, engaging in no activity. In the early period after the victory in the War of Resistance, my friend Qi Qingbin, who took up the post of chief of the inspection department of the “Beiping Garrison Headquarters,” was likewise the former secretary of the “Shanghai District.” We three were not only comrades and colleagues but bound by a deep private friendship; and so, though my friend Qi Qingbin presided at Beiping over the rooting-out of traitors, yet toward Zhang Zuoxing, who had once held a puppet post, he did not, so long as no one denounced him, pursue the matter of his own accord.

I of course had to contrive his deliverance, and no better road offered than the winning of merit before the enemy. With the deputy brigade commander’s understanding, I employed him—yet keeping hidden that passage of his history related above. Little did I think a problem would remain even so: for to employ a man, one must report him and place him on record, or else he is a “black” man; and to report him to one’s superiors for the record, one must attach detailed personnel particulars, and should those particulars be false, that too is a trouble. So Zhang Zuoxing, though already a commanding officer in the brigade, was to this time never formally appointed.
If anyone should reproach me over this matter for shielding him and bending the rules for a private end, I have thought upon it: better silence than to argue in my own defense.

In the tenth chapter of the fourth part I set down how, in the thirty-second year, the writer prevailed upon his old friend Yin Qingyu to break through the blockade line back to the great rear, and there find the director of the “Southeast Office of the Juntong Bureau,” my friend Mao Wanli, to restore our working connection; which was settled at last at Yanshan in Jiangxi, where I had the kindness of my friend Wanli in dispatching his captain-adjutant Li Yao to return with my friend Yin to Shanghai and convey a message by word of mouth. Now Li Yao had resigned his post at Hangzhou and, with my friend Wanli’s consent likewise, had come to Beiping. Li Yao prided himself not a little on his marksmanship; and let us see how he shows himself. For the present he was employed provisionally as captain-adjutant, pending transfer to a suitable post.

There were, besides, four men, old colleagues who had once shared hardship and peril with me: the seasoned intelligence editors Mao Yilu and Huang Wei; the gifted draftsman Hong Fuyu; and Zhou Qiqing, who was skilled both at Chinese typewriting and at managing accounts. They wrote to say that they all had a great mind to come to Beiping, and I too wished to work again alongside them. But they were at that time serving members of the “Third Section of the Shanghai Station,” and could not, of course, go wherever they took a fancy. As it happened—did I not hold concurrently the post of leader of the “Beiping directly subordinate section”? So under that name I requested their transfer to come and “handle intelligence,” adding the declaration that all their emoluments would be borne wholly by me here. This move worked to a marvel: the request was granted no sooner than made. When they had come, I, as a temporary expedient, first arranged the enrollment of the four in the brigade—that is, they ate the brigade’s rations and drew the brigade’s pay. Of them, Zhou Qiqing and Hong Fuyu lived within the brigade, Zhou assisting in the commissariat and Hong devoting himself to the drawing of charts and tables; while Mao Yilu and Huang Wei rented lodgings apart, and gave themselves wholly to the “intelligence direction” of the “Beiping directly subordinate section.” For one could by no means, in a muddle, mix up the business of two units together.

The “Third Section of the Shanghai Station” mentioned above had a deep origin with me: its forerunner was the “Third Station of the Shanghai District,” whose chief at that time was likewise myself. This was a matter of after the victory in the War of Resistance. Before that, we all worked at No. 99 Yidingpan Road in Shanghai, “No. 99” for short; on the surface it was the “First Committee” cooperating with the Japanese side, but in fact it was the “Seventh Station” of the “Juntong Bureau,” whose chief was also myself. There were then some twenty-odd men, and those who came this time from Shanghai were four of their number.

Perhaps the book will have no occasion to set down the things that befell after the reorganization of the brigade headquarters, and so I would note here in advance: that some years later Mao Yilu (also named Mao Zihou) died on the border between Macau and the mainland, and Huang Wei died in the city of Guangzhou—both of them fell in the struggle against Communism, neither yet forty years of age; and it is my regret that in no record whatever will their names be found. In the spring of the thirty-fifth year, during the several months I was held in the Shanghai Municipal Detention House, though I was not free to move about, yet I made no few friends; and to speak in earnest, the friends made at such a juncture are indeed friends whose fellowship is felt the more. Among these new friends, the staff of the detention house (clerks, orderlies, guards, and the like) outnumbered even my fellow prisoners of the same “schooling.” Why? Because my standing in the “Juntong Bureau” was very senior, and my case a singular one, so that they rather knew who I was, and had, besides, no little interest in learning what I had done. As I have told in the last section of the fourth part of my humble work, they had sympathy for me—so far, even, as recklessly to slip me in secret the very key of the cell door, that it might help me to break out in an hour of emergency.

When I returned this time to Beiping, they, hearing the news, followed the trail and came—six or seven of them, arriving one after another. Beyond welcoming them with all my heart, I gave each a fitting placement. Of course, each had his own strength and his own charge, and each could fulfill his duty; by no means did they come to seek a lucky chance on the strength of their private connection with me. Yet in all this there was, inevitably, some small vexation.

I have considered that it is better still not to disclose the names of these six or seven men; my concern is that the greater part of them are to this day holding public office in Taiwan, and are soon to reach the age of retirement, and I would not bring upon them any needless trouble. As for that debt of kindness which each of them laid upon me—it is a thing I shall never dare to forget.

Besides these, there were still others—for the most part the sons and younger brothers of old friends and well-wishers. Counting them off on my fingers, there were, first and last, a good many batches, some come from afar, some from the near environs. I explained to them in all sincerity: that life here was hard and the pay meager; that not only were the rules strict, it was fraught with danger besides; and that even should I wish to bend things to look after them, I might not be able to do it very thoroughly—better, then, to think it well over. So I said; yet the younger generation cared not a whit, and at the mention of danger, it was as though only then was there thrill enough.

These young people did not, one and all, necessarily understand what it was to oppose Communism, and as for pacification and the suppression of rebellion, of that they were the more unversed. But once they were set upon the road, they would work at it the more keenly. This is a fact, in no way exaggerated. It may serve to show how very strong is the malleability of the young: whether they would incline to the left or to the right hereafter depended wholly on their environment.

Of these young people who joined the force at that time there were some twenty-odd; and it must be said that, after a spell of hard tempering, what with the missing, the captured, and those who fell away from the ranks, of those now in Taiwan there remain but a scant few. Their average age is now about fifty-eight or fifty-nine, and some may yet be living on the mainland; and so I do not set down their names either.

All these many men had a direct connection with me; and besides them, no few came by way of introduction—such as Pang Zhaofeng, recommended by my friend Zhang Zuoxing; Liu Wenxun, brought in by a friend outside the brigade, one Mr. Wang; and comrades Zhang Xiaopu and Wei Jun, who were introduced from hand to hand into this brigade. They were all officers on active service, come either out of the Northeast Military Academy or graduated from the Central Military Academy, and so all held important posts.

The deputy brigade commander Li recommended but one, my friend Li Changqing, who was a good deal older than we, but a veteran of the ranks and of no little discernment, and had held colonel’s rank many years; hampered by the establishment, I could only ask him to condescend to the post of brigade adjutant, to be adjusted hereafter when the establishment should be enlarged.

Talented men from the four quarters and the eight came thronging one upon another, greatly strengthening the force’s power and showing forth a vigor and abundance, a flourishing and thriving—a good sign indeed. Yet in this there was a flaw as well: namely, that between the newly joined and those who had received training there was, in many respects, no perfect harmony. It did not go so far as mutual incompatibility, or an inability to cooperate; but in ideology there was always some gap—that is, in ways of thinking and of doing they could not yet be wholly of one accord.

To put it from yet another angle: to have the untrained direct those who had been trained was not very fitting either; and so in the end, saving a few outstanding instances, in the performance of the work it was an unalterable fact both that the old hands were not the equal of the fresh talents, and that the trained were stronger than the untrained.

During the training of the “Lizhi Class,” the “bandit situation” was also an important course of study; but the time was too short, and in a situation that changed from instant to instant, one always felt that what one understood was not enough, and wanting in practicality. This was a great defect, and a fact not to be gainsaid.

The “bandit situation” is the “enemy situation”; to have the enemy situation in hand was our proper office. Since it was to fight the Communist Party and to destroy the Communist Party, we had of course to understand the Communist Party through and through. And the depth or shallowness of that understanding was precisely the greatest factor deciding success or failure.

Among the First Brigade’s tasks, the work area designated by our superiors was fairly vast, comprising the three provinces of Hebei, Chahar, and Suiyuan, the two cities of Beiping and Tianjin, and further the line from Gubeikou to the city of Chengde in Rehe Province. This was a great trial in the deployment of manpower. And of the enemy situation in the regions above listed we had no systematic understanding, being still far from the degree at which it could be put to use.

By the ordinary procedure, before parceling out and dispatching men, one must of course assign them their tasks, and at the same time must give them some indication of the basic conditions of the region. Yet even this our brigade headquarters found doubly thorny.

I knew that at Beiping those who ought to have an understanding of the enemy situation were: first, the Second Section of the “Beiping Field Headquarters,” since their chief business was intelligence; and second, the “Beiping Station” under the “Baomiju,” intelligence work being a part of their labors too.

In point of “working relation,” since the “First Brigade of the Pacification Corps” was attached to the “Beiping Field Headquarters,” the “Beiping Field Headquarters” had both the authority to supervise and direct the “First Brigade” and, at the same time, the responsibility to assist it. Hence to furnish the bandit-situation material we needed was a thing that followed in the natural course. Moreover the chief of the Field Headquarters’ Second Section, my friend Zhang Jiaquan, was an old working partner of more than ten years before, and could do it without asking leave. The only question was how much “accuracy” and “applicability” the bandit-situation material in their hands possessed. Still, it was, on the whole, a help to us.

As for the head of the other secret unit, he too was an old friend; but he could not furnish intelligence to us directly, and must have his superior’s approval first—which made it troublesome; and so, knowing the difficulty, I stopped short.

Speaking of understanding the “bandit situation,” I myself had some foundation earlier, in my Shanghai days; but I had had no contact with it for a good two years and more, so that I was not only out of joint with it but of course could not keep up with its changes. Even had I striven hard to catch up, being limited by time, I could not have done it in a short span.
Though Mao Yilu and Huang Wei, newly transferred from the “Third Section of the Shanghai Station,” were rather familiar with the bandit situation, this too was confined to the South China region.

Happily these two had for some years past been handling intelligence bearing on the Chinese Communists, and had, more or less, some basic understanding; this of itself was not enough to meet the present need, but it still served us for reference. What was of use to us just then was the political intrigues of the Chinese Communists in the Beiping-Tianjin region, together with the military movements—and the strategy adopted—of the forces of Lin Biao and Nie Rongzhen, within and beyond the Pass.

To put it more concretely, we divided the current gathering and distribution of intelligence into three tiers. The first was that which could serve our own use—that is, what the several units of this brigade required in carrying out their other work: pacification, action, assault. This, in principle, ought to be gathered by each command room for itself, according to local conditions, and used of its own motion. Where, among it, there was material bearing upon other working units, that too might be shared for mutual reference and use.

The second was that which could serve for the reference and use of the “Beiping Field Headquarters,” the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,” and, transmitted through the Corps Headquarters, the Ministry of National Defense.

Since it is now a thing of the past, I will note by the way here: the one in charge of intelligence business at the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” was of course the Second Section, whose chief, Shi Hong, was by usage recommended by the “Juntong,” and whom the commander-in-chief of the “North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters” by usage accepted. But he was very small-minded—or one might say he had his own designs—and set the center of gravity of intelligence upon the Third Section, which was in charge of combat business, because he held that these were his own trusted intimates; and he actually put the Second Section in a subordinate, dependent place, giving it no weight. Consider: to gather a single piece of intelligence of operational value—how hard a thing that is, sometimes to be got only at the risk of one’s very life—and should it meet with such a case as the above, is it not all thrown away for nothing?

The third was strategic intelligence, also called high-grade intelligence; precious because so hard to come by, it was commonly a thing there was but little chance to obtain. Since the gathering of intelligence was our chief mission, we ought to set our efforts squarely toward this mark. And so a few of us did just that.

This passage of the story, in the telling, may seem a thing rather shadowy and unreal; yet, saving that some of its course I can no longer clearly recall, the whole of it is fact, true beyond all doubt.

In the posthumous work of the Corps Commander, Mr. Liu Peichu, Fleeting Glimpses of a Floating Life, there are a few words that point to this very matter. The book states: “Left-leaning persons were once made use of to attain the end of obtaining strategic intelligence, and the Ministry of National Defense twice bestowed on the First Brigade of the Pacification Corps prize money of very great amount.”

The substance of the matter and the course of it were roughly as follows. The conception and the design: to make the gathering of strategic intelligence the main thing, and, as occasion offered, to induce leading elements of the Chinese Communists to come over. This was no putting of the cart before the horse; it took the higher or lower degree of possibility as its ground—otherwise it would have been mere wishful thinking.

Those who took part in it: besides the writer himself, there were my two schoolmates Jiang Tian and Zhang Zuoxing, newly come to work in this brigade. There was, besides, one schoolmate Li Mingqiu, who, though he took part in this affair, yet stood on a footing not the same as ours three.

The objects chosen: three men in all, all of them leaders of the Chinese Communists, being, in order of the height of their posts, Lin Biao, commander of the Chinese Communist “Northeast People’s Liberation Army”; Tao Zhu, director of the Political Department of the Chinese Communist “Northeast People’s Liberation Army”; and Li Yunchang, deputy political commissar of the ——th Column of the Chinese Communist “North China People’s Liberation Army.”

At that time, in the thirty-sixth or thirty-seventh year, the standing of the three men—Lin, Tao, and Li—within the Chinese Communist Central (Party) was reckoned none too high; but afterward Lin Biao shot up, rising to be “Vice-Chairman,” but half a head below Mao Zedong, and by “explicit ordinance” became Mao Zedong’s “successor.” Where the malady lay one cannot tell, but Lin Biao would not wait for Mao Zedong to fall or die betimes, and rose in revolt before his time, meaning to overthrow Mao Zedong and set himself up; wherein he failed, and died in a manner dark and unexplained, which to this day remains a riddle.

Tao Zhu first became “Governor of Guangdong,” and afterward shot up too, to member of the “Politburo of the CCP Central Committee” and head of the “Propaganda Department of the CCP Central Committee,” ranking fourth in turn within the Chinese Communist leading group. In the year Beiping was in the turmoil of the “Red Guards,” Tao too was struggled against at his residence in Zhongnanhai, and was in the end banished to a concentration camp in Anhui for “remolding,” where before long he died of lung cancer.
Li Yunchang’s standing was lower; he was once “elected” an alternate member of the “CCP Central Committee” and head of the “Ministry of Railways,” but never rose higher after that.
Having thus briefly set forth these three men, that one may have some notion of them, let me next begin from the personal relations among us all.
The relations among us: the first thing to make clear is that these relations, so called, were confined to old private connections. And a connection was, of course, one means of contriving contact.
In the foregoing section I have already introduced my two schoolmates Jiang Tian and Zhang Zuoxing; besides us three in this affair, let me now briefly introduce this schoolmate Li Mingqiu.

Li Mingqiu was a man of Zunhua in Hebei. When he enlisted at the Military Academy, he too was a recruit in the Ninth Company of the First Regiment, in the same company as Jiang Tian and Zhang Zuoxing.
At that time (the fifteenth year of the Republic) Li Mingqiu had already joined the Communist Party, and was deputy secretary of the “regimental committee” of the First Regiment.
Lin Biao was a recruit in the Fifth Company of the First Regiment, and a Communist too, and they would often gather in little knots of threes and fives for their furtive meetings.
The place was either up in a hollow of Shougou Ridge, or deep within a thicket of bamboo. So already at that time they were well acquainted.

Every Sunday Li Mingqiu, Lin Biao, and the rest would be sure to go to Dongshan in the outskirts of Guangzhou to take part in a meeting; and it is known that the Chinese Communist “secretary of the Military Commission” at that time was none other than Zhou Enlai.

When Li Mingqiu left the Military Academy, the Communist Party sent him to Tianjin for secret work; he was arrested and imprisoned, held nine years, and did not come out until the twenty-fifth year of the Republic. One day we met near the Quanyechang in Tianjin, and he did not know that I was the chief of the “Tianjin Station.” Old schoolmates meeting again in a strange place, I invited him to the Shandong restaurant Dengyinglou for a banquet at sixteen dollars a table, and asked Wang Wen, Zeng Che, and others to keep us company; and halfway through the meal he fell to weeping. Calling to mind the bitterness of his years in prison, he reproached me to my face for the corruption of my way of living.
I had a mind to win him over to join our work, but he declared he would do nothing at all any more, and would go back to his native place to nurse his health before aught else.

Li Mingqiu’s native place was Zunhua, and Zhang Zuoxing’s native place was Zunhua too; they were not only schoolmates but fellow-townsmen of the same small district, and from this time on they kept in touch.

In the twenty-seventh year, during the War of Resistance, I was ordered to raise guerrillas behind the enemy’s lines, and set up the “Luan-Yu Guerrilla Headquarters,” presently renamed the “North China Loyal and Patriotic Army,” with Zhang Zuoxing as director of the Political Department, spreading guerrilla activity through the East Hebei region. At that time Li Mingqiu was still recuperating in the countryside, and I invited him to join in and share the nation’s peril. He gave his assent; but whether he had by then resumed his organizational tie with the Communist Party, I cannot say for certain.

Before the founding of the “Luan-Yu Headquarters,” the “North China Loyal and Patriotic Army,” there had already appeared many small bands of guerrilla forces in the region about Shanhaiguan (Linyu) and in the mountains within and without the Great Wall; because provisioning was hard, the environment set limits to the survival and growth of any large body of troops, yet being set in remote places, they escaped the Japanese army’s “mopping-up.”

One of these bands, of some two or three hundred men only, was headed by none other than Li Yunchang. Li Yunchang too was a man of Zunhua, of the same clan as Li Mingqiu, and by the genealogy of the same generation—that is, a distant cousin. After a deal of go-between work by Li Mingqiu, Li Yunchang accepted the title the “Luan-Yu Headquarters” gave him, and at the same time was forever asking us for support.

At that time, whether Li Yunchang was a Communist—though his every act was very like it—was not gone into deeply. For in those days the ardor to fight the Japanese devils ran hot, while guarding against the infiltration of Communist elements was not held very strictly. In matters of this kind we ought to admit that there was indeed a carelessness, an inexperience, a lowness of vigilance.

Later, when the “Loyal and Patriotic Headquarters” was set up in the home of Wang Wen (“Tianjin Station” action-group leader, and commander of the ——th Route of the “North China Loyal and Patriotic Army”) in Baodi County, it met the fierce artillery fire of a Japanese regiment, and thereby suffered a grievous sapping of its vital strength, from which for a long time it could not recover.

Not long after, the writer was ordered transferred away; the acting chief of the “Tianjin Station,” Zeng Che, was arrested and killed, Wang Wen too died a cruel death at the poisoned hands of the Japanese gendarmerie, and the “North China Loyal and Patriotic Army” likewise fell and could not rise again. By this present time, Li Yunchang was still active in the East Hebei region, and had already grown strong.

Two years further on, when the writer was reading “bandit-situation material” in the “Shanghai District,” I found that Li Yunchang had already become the commander of some “military sub-district” of the Communist forces. As to whether he had gone over to the Communists long before, or had merely shown his true colors, I did not probe further. And Li Mingqiu had long since been lost from contact, his whereabouts unknown.
The above sets forth, to begin with, the relation of the writer, Jiang Tian, and Zhang Zuoxing with Li Mingqiu, and the relations of Li Mingqiu with Lin Biao, and of Li Mingqiu with Li Yunchang.
What follows tells further of the relation of Jiang Tian with Lin Biao.

The recruits’ First Regiment was divided into three battalions and twelve companies, all quartered in the barracks-ground at Shahe in the near suburbs of Guangzhou. The “barracks-ground,” so called, was no more than rows upon rows of thatched sheds. The whole regiment drilled together on one great parade-ground, but each company had its own lecture hall; and if the whole regiment assembled, that too was held on the great parade-ground, for there was no great auditorium such as one commonly has today.

Lin Biao was in the Fifth Company of the Second Battalion; Jiang Tian, Zhang Zuoxing, and Li Mingqiu were all in the Ninth Company of the Third Battalion; and the writer was in the Tenth Company of the Third Battalion.

The barracks of company and company adjoined one another, but between battalion and battalion a distance of twenty or thirty paces was set. Jiang Tian, Zhang Zuoxing, and I had no contact whatever with Lin Biao. We few were Northerners, while Lin Biao was a man of Hubei, and in our off-duty personal pursuits we did not fall in together either, so that we had the less occasion to become acquainted. And Li Mingqiu, when he was ordinarily among us, never spoke of that whole furtive business of Lin Biao and his set.

Not half a year into the recruit training at Shahe, the whole regiment was ordered to shift its defense to Huizhou and Huiyang. I remember only that the Ninth and Tenth Companies were quartered in the Confucius Temple, holding the neighborhood of the Little South Gate; of the other companies I am not clear.

Before long the advancement examination was held, and Jiang Tian and Li Mingqiu passed up—these were the fourth term of the Military Academy. Zhang Zuoxing and I failed the examination, had our recruit training prolonged, and by the time we advanced were of the fifth term. Lin Biao had passed up into the Academy proper at the same time as Jiang Tian and the rest, and it was through being in the same branch and the same squad that they came to know one another.
Thereafter, during my time at the Academy, I never once saw Jiang Tian or Li Mingqiu again.

By the twenty-first year, was it?—it was in an inn near the New Station in Tianjin that I met Jiang Tian; and it was not until the twenty-fifth year, as I have said above, that on the main street below the Quanyechang in the French Concession of Tianjin I ran into Li Mingqiu. By this time I had long since clean forgotten the name of Lin Biao.
To tell now of my relation with Tao Zhu.

My prolonged enlistment brought me from Huizhou back again to Shahe. I was assigned to the Eleventh Company of the Third Battalion, whose designation was, it seems, still the recruits’ First Regiment.

The regimental commander was Wang Wenhan (?); the Third Battalion commander was Li Jingnan, of the first term of the Military Academy; and the Eleventh Company commander was Lu Junquan, of the Yunnan Military Academy. The whole company numbered about 120 men, and among them was one Tao Zhu.

I remember that we advanced without an examination, and so came from Shahe to the Academy’s main seat—that is, the world-famous “Whampoa.” Tao Zhu and I were both assigned to the Second Squadron of the First Student Brigade; the brigade commander was Shuai Chongxing, of the Yunnan Military Academy; the Second Squadron commander was Hui Ji, of the Baoding Officers’ School; and the squad leader was Wang Dengti, of the ——th term of the Military Academy.

In April of the sixteenth year came the “Party Purge.” On that day, in the dimness of dawn, I heard the bugle, and listening close made out that it was not reveille but the emergency-assembly call; thereupon the officer of the day gave his order and the whistle sounded all together, saying, “No arms to be borne—assemble where you stand.” At once I dressed and bound on my puttees, and in but three or five minutes all had, as on any other day, fallen into their ranks to await the roll. Then came the word of command: “Objective the Great Lecture Hall—forward march!” We felt sure some incident had occurred. The Great Lecture Hall was newly built and could hold several hundred; and there we saw a great dark press of them, the students already standing packed within. At the very center of the platform stood the Dean of Studies, Fang Dingying, a white towel wrapped about his neck, gesturing with his hand, as though asking Wu Siyu, the head of the Training Department, who stood at one side, to preside. Only afterward did I hear that Dean Fang was suffering from a sore throat.

Wu Siyu first saluted Fang Dingying, strode a few paces forward, and in that sharp voice peculiar to him cried out “Attention”; then he turned and saluted Dean Fang again, and the salute done, turned back and cried “At ease.” There was a silence of some seconds, and then I heard him proclaim the order: “All of you hear this! Whoever has joined the Communist Party—fall out!” From afar came only the sound of footsteps; near at hand, Tao Zhu, Wan Limin, He Kun, and others of our squad all stepped forth.

The falling-out was done swiftly, and in an instant all was quiet again. Head Wu Siyu spoke again in plain words: “All who have fallen out, come to the front—at the double!” I saw only Tao Zhu’s retreating back, and from that time knew not where he had gone.

Afterward I heard that they were in all some hundred and thirty or forty men, held at first on five wooden boats moored in mid-river, watched over from alongside by the gunboat Zhongshan, and later removed to Humen. From that time I heard no more news of him. In the summer of the nineteenth year of the Republic, when I was going from Xinxiang to Kaifeng to visit kin and, passing through Zhengzhou, changed trains, I unexpectedly met Tao Zhu on the railway platform; however great the change, I could not have mistaken the man. He was alone, wasted in his looks, yet his clothes were still neat, and by the look of him he was either waiting for someone or waiting for a train. When he saw me he did not avoid me, but hastened over to take my hand, shaking it and clapping me hard on the shoulder, as though in his bearing the old feeling lingered still.

One could see he was not well-off, nor was I flush; we bought a few steamed buns, found a place where big bowls of tea were drunk, and sitting face to face on a long bench, fell to talking. He asked me where I was going, and I told him to Kaifeng; I asked him, but he would not answer me, and only smiled.

Tao Zhu spoke of the past. He said, “After I got aboard the boat that morning, there was nothing but eating and sleeping; one night, when the river was at full tide, some twenty and more swam off and got away. The next day ten or so were caught and brought back, held, it was said, at Hudiegang, and never came back to the boat again.” He said again, “The hundred and more of us who were left were removed to a newly built prison at the Humen Fortress, at the Shanghengdang Battery—say nothing of locking the cell door, for even had they opened the gate and let us walk out, on all four sides was the sea (the mouth of the Pearl River): where was one to run?” I asked him, “How long were you at Humen—did no one question you?” He went on, “At Humen about three months, and then removed to Guangzhou, held for the time being in the lockup of the Public Security Bureau, and by then it was already the end of November and the beginning of December. Rumor was that the trial was about to begin, yet there was no sign of movement.” Tao Zhu glanced about him, before and behind and to either side, and dragging the bench a little closer, leaned in and asked me in a low voice, “The great December-Twelfth Guangzhou Uprising—do you know of it or not?” I asked him back, “And if I do?” He said, “Our whole band broke out that very night, and those who took us in were the very men who had swum off the boats.” I asked, “And after you got out?” He said, “We chose Squad Leader Zhong (the writer notes: Zhong Qiguang, third term of the Military Academy, and a Communist, once served as president of the Chinese Communist ‘Military Academy’) to lead us; we assembled first at the North Parade Ground, and then joined the ranks of battle.” Tao Zhu paused and said again, “It held out but a single day and night before it could not be sustained and collapsed. I fled first to Haifeng, and then by roundabout ways reached Jiangxi.” The one question I could not but ask: “What are you doing now?” He bowed his head, his eyes not meeting mine, and said with his lips, “Just drifting!” I saw through him and said, “The devil himself would believe it.” The talk having come to this, there was nothing more to be said. And so I went on to my Kaifeng, and from that time his news was cut off from me. Now he is director of the Political Department of the Chinese Communist “Northeast People’s Liberation Army”; and besides what has been found in intelligence material, it has been carried in the newspapers too.
This, then, is the personal relation between Tao Zhu and me.

Putting together all that is said above, one may draw out a line that could be turned to use, namely: my own, Jiang Tian’s, and Zhang Zuoxing’s tie with Li Mingqiu; Jiang Tian’s and Li Mingqiu’s tie with Lin Biao; Li Mingqiu’s and Zhang Zuoxing’s tie with Li Yunchang; and my own tie with Tao Zhu.
Since there was this many-sided web of relations, one had to lay some plan, to gain from it an advantage for the work.

In the four parts of my humble work already published, whenever a story formed a unit of its own, I have always told it in order of time, unwinding it layer by layer as one draws silk from the cocoon; the upshot being that a whole story was cut into several pieces, with something of the air of holding back the point for suspense. In truth this way of it must be said to have its good and its bad. This time I mean to write the story out from head to tail at a single breath, short and to the point. Though it overleaps the order of time, it is well that all of it is past matter, so that a little inversion of before and after does no great harm.
Before I resolved to go forward with this affair, the first consideration was how strictly to keep the secret, and so it could not be handled by the ordinary procedure.

Of the men of the brigade, only I, Jiang Tian, and Zhang Zuoxing knew the bottom of it; not even the deputy brigade commander was informed—for fear he might grow suspicious, I made only the slightest hint of a disclosure, and he of course inquired no further.

Yet it had to be reported to my superiors for the record; otherwise, should some slip occur, there would be the suspicion of “communicating with the enemy,” and then, say what one might, one could never explain it clearly.

This “reporting for the record,” so called, is to report by word of mouth or in writing to the superior in charge, who, after examination, replies with “permitted to be filed for reference”—only then are the formalities complete. For the sake of having proof and warrant, it was commonly done in writing more often than not. Even a telegraphic cipher had to be put into written words, and still counted as a written document. And thus it must, come what may, pass through the hands of a clerk who handled it—which I held to be unsound even so.

And so I had no choice but to go over the head of the Corps Headquarters and report in person, by word of mouth, to Mr. Zheng Jiemin. In my eyes, he alone had the boldness for it, dared to take it upon himself. Though this already constituted a reporting over the levels, which ought not to be done, yet I had a responsibility to make sure that this affair should proceed in perfect safety.

There was yet another reason: on this affair I had to seek Mr. Zheng Jiemin’s instruction as to the fitting course; for Mr. Zheng’s understanding of the Chinese Communists was the deepest, and he was at the same time the one who executed the use of stratagem against them, so that by putting in a report beforehand and setting the matter out clearly, I might avoid the playing-out of “overlap” or “collision”—though the likelihood of that was not high, it was not a thing to leave unguarded against. And then there was the psychological preparation proper to myself. Should it fail, the responsibility would of course be mine; and should some achievement be won, great or small, there had to be someone to receive it too. How is this to be understood? Because it was not work assigned by my superiors, and so it needed their assent and acknowledgment.
A layer deeper than this it is not fitting to explain in written words. Cases of the like may now and then be seen in the reports of international news.

At that time Mr. Zheng Jiemin was in Nanjing, and I in Beiping; since letter and telegram were both inconvenient, there was nothing for it but to make a journey to Nanjing. Yet, having my duties upon me, I could not, unless with leave, go this way and that wherever I took a fancy; and the best plan was none other than to divide it into two steps—first to begin the preparatory work, and to contrive an occasion to meet with Mr. Zheng.

After many deliberations among us three, the most important move in the preparatory work was to seek out a person who could go about on our behalf. The qualifications for this person were rather “harsh,” and such a one was naturally hard to find. What, then, were the qualifications? First: not a serving member of this brigade—that is, a man outside the brigade. Besides avoiding the drawing-on of needless misunderstanding, there was in it the care to guard against giving others a handle.

Second: a man whom the other side would receive without doing him harm. This, of course, was fittest in one who had old ties with the other side. Were he an utter stranger, there would not only be resistance—he might not so much as get to see the object at all, and, worse, there would be the risk of his being “detained.”
Third: this man must have some courage, and wit enough, or how was he to meet with barrier upon barrier of difficulty, and above all to pass through the blockade lines of the combat zones?
Fourth: he must have a bond of friendship with some one of us three.
Fifth: the man must possess certain ordinary faculties besides—such as powers of observation, of judgment, of memory, and the like.
Where, then, was such a man to be found? We three were of one mind that the most ideal was our schoolmate Li Mingqiu.

But ever since our guerrilla failure in the East Hebei region in the twenty-eighth year of the Republic, when we had scattered forthwith, where Li Mingqiu might be was to this day unknown. And now that Li’s native place, Zunhua, had fallen into the hands of the Communist forces, to seek news of him was the harder still.

Zhang Zuoxing too was a man of Zunhua; his thought was that, to seek news of Li, it were best first to ask among the fellow-townsmen in Beiping and Tianjin, and if nothing could be got out of them, then to find some fellow-townsman in trade to make a journey to Zunhua—and should he chance upon one just come up from Zunhua, better still.

Asking in Beiping and Tianjin after this Li Mingqiu, nine in ten knew nothing of him, and the one who did know him said too that he had not seen him for years. As for men come out of Zunhua, such there were, but none of them meant to go back again (by now Zunhua had fallen into the bandits’ hands). The last resort was to find someone to go back to Zunhua.

A man to go back to Zunhua was indeed found, whom here I can only stand for by the name of “Elder Cousin.” Reckoning it up—though he is now past eighty, it may be he is yet living on the mainland; and moreover he has a whole brood of sons and daughters, none of whom came out, so that should I bring consequences upon him it would be too grievous a sin. “Elder Cousin” was willing to make the journey for us, and reckoned himself fairly sure that he could “get back in” and “get out again.” The seeking of Li Mingqiu’s whereabouts had at last a footing, and one could only hope the man who went would be able to find him.

Another piece of preparatory work was to learn where the headquarters of the Chinese Communist “Northeast People’s Liberation Army” lay; for to know where their headquarters was, was to be able to find Lin Biao and Tao Zhu.
News concerning Li Yunchang could never be verified, which was perhaps by reason of his too great mobility.

This case ran over a fairly long stretch of time, from the planning begun at the end of the thirty-sixth year down to the autumn of the thirty-seventh. At the point of which I now speak, it was about the first or second month of the thirty-seventh year—that is, around the Spring Festival.
It comes back to me: before he set out, “Elder Cousin” had laid in no little store of New Year goods, saying that he must at all costs hasten back in time to keep the New Year.

Consulting the records: since the first month of the thirty-seventh year, the forces of Lin Biao, who had usurped and held the Northeast, were launching a large-scale offensive against our army, and forthwith took Goubangzi, severing the line of communication between Shenyang and Jinzhou. Judging from this, Lin Biao himself must likewise be somewhere in this neighborhood.

At the very end of the old year, “Elder Cousin” did indeed return safe and sound—I can only say that he possessed a “natural protective coloring,” and will add no more. The news he brought back said, “Li Mingqiu is weak and much ailing, and is now keeping accounts in a cloth shop in Tianjin. Of the rest I did not ask much.” The address and the sign of this cloth shop I had, but by now have long forgotten them. Zhang Zuoxing made a special journey there, and did indeed find Li Mingqiu; but before Zhang Zuoxing could tell out his errand, Li refused in a word. My friend Zuoxing, helpless, could only invite him to come to Beiping, and this too Li would not; in the end he said that when the weather grew warm, he would find an occasion for us all to gather together again.

My friend Zuoxing came back and told it to me, and I could only take him with me and go once more to Tianjin. Happily the Ping-Jin Railway was still open at this time, and by the through express, one-way, it was two hours’ journey. Counting in the time of boarding and alighting and of going to and from the stations, one could make the round trip in five or six hours; and with the delay of the business added, setting out at noon, one could surely hasten back by eight in the evening. That is to say, leaving the brigade headquarters in the afternoon and showing myself again by ten at night would rouse no notice.

On the train, my friend Zuoxing and I spoke of the question whether Li Mingqiu might take the old road again (meaning the resuming of his organizational tie with the Communist Party). My friend Zuoxing could pass no judgment, but by his view, that a man come out of the Military Academy should, of all things, be helping keep accounts in a cloth shop, seemed always somewhat to invite suspicion.

After we reached Tianjin, we drew Li Mingqiu out to meet us, and it cost I know not how much talk—by the end our discussing had turned into entreaty—before he unbent a little and agreed to be given a day or two’s time, to consider it closely. At the last he declared, “You must lay no trap to cozen me into joining your work.” When next we met he was not so distant as before; we spoke of old times, and touched on the present too, and talking on and on, came to the situation of the moment. He sighed in dejection: “A man past forty, and nothing accomplished, fallen too far behind—I can keep up with none of it now.” He said again, “It is wholly those nine years of prison that broke my body down; my health once gone, what is there left worth pursuing? Could I but travel, I would have gone off with them long ago.” Once the talk was fairly opened, it was like the sluice-gates of the Yellow River flung wide—there was no damming it; and the sum of his mind was this: that he still could not put the Communist Party out of his heart, and that his not taking part in actual activity was wholly by reason of his failing strength.

As for why he was stuck in a cloth shop eating an idle meal and drawing a few coppers—it was no more than to get through the days and scrape a living. He said plainly himself, “Do not suppose that I am using the cloth shop as a screen and still carrying on that game underneath; in very truth I have not done it for years.” He added a further word: “And were I still at it, what harm even in my owning it?” These words of his, if it were purely a matter of friendship, one could not but believe; only because this was not an affair of the private feeling between one man and another—even if he were to be believed, my duty being what it was, I could not but hold back a few parts of my trust.

His declaration of position done, the talk came to the main point, and Li Mingqiu’s words were startling—this was no jesting matter now. He said, “Is it not that you hope I will make a journey beyond the Pass (meaning the Northeast)? I have considered it: go I will, but I cannot bear such cold; ten days or a fortnight hence, when the weather is a little warmer, only then can I set out.” In such a matter, though the sooner the better, since he said so, one could only bend to the fact—wait, then, we would.

He said again, “If you cherish the hope that I will persuade Lin and Tao to revolt before the battle-line, that will be hard; not only will they not do so, I will not so speak either.
