It is no throwing of cold water—you had best kill that hope at the outset.” This was nothing; who did not know that, at that very hour, should Lin Biao indeed stage a revolt before the line and come over to our side, the great tide of things could be turned about at once, and the reach of it, at a single stroke, settle the whole board? Yet how should we not understand too that this was mere wishful thinking—that where there was no “sowing of the cause,” whence should come the “sudden change”?

Li Mingqiu said in all solemnity, “If your intent is to lay a road for your survival hereafter, or to establish an understanding by which each may keep the other informed, then you are right, and I shall be the more willing to go about for you.” Having said these few words, he did not wait for our response, but pressed straight on: “Beyond this, what do you bid me go and do? And for what am I doing it?” He showed himself so firm and set—how then was one to deal with it?
From the standpoint of the work, the qualifications Li Mingqiu possessed were really too good; the thing must on no account be let come to a deadlock.

Yet neither could I agree to his consideration—even were it a matter of “means to an end,” before I had my superiors’ sanction it was on no account to be done; this was very plain, and any slight error would breed consequences of ruin and disgrace.

The plan for the present was only to put it off a few days and take it up again; and so I answered Li Mingqiu, “Today Jiang Tian has not come. Wait until I have met with him and asked his view, and then we will talk it over with you.” As things now stood, the active part had turned into the passive; but come what might, one could not for all that let go and, for nothing, lose a chance.

At Beiping, Zhang Zuoxing, Jiang Tian, and I, we three, exchanged views upon that speech Li Mingqiu had put forth. The two of them were not of one mind either: the one held for agreeing to him by word of mouth, and leaving all until there had been contact—contact failing, all talk was empty; the other held for going once more to Li Mingqiu, first reasoning it out with him, and then telling him our intent flat out—go if he would, and let it be if he would not.

I drew no conclusion, nor needed to; for within my heart I had already decided: so long as Li Mingqiu could go, be it “for old times’ sake,” be it “to lay a road,” be it “to keep each other informed,” let Li say what he would.
What was sought was this: to find where Lin and Tao were; to get to see Lin and Tao themselves, or either one of the two; and to make contact as much as might be—saying little and hearing much.
Whatever the outcome, I asked only that he should tell me faithfully all he saw along the way, and every word and phrase of Lin and Tao—that alone would make the journey not made in vain.
Besides, it were best that I could see Mr. Zheng before Li set out; and if there were not time, that too must be with all speed.

Li’s character was very strong, and on no account would he come to Beiping, so that we three could only go by turns to accommodate him. Before he set out, the matter of Li Yunchang was mentioned too; he said he did not know where the man was, and to avoid raising fresh complications, we laid it aside for the time and spoke of it no more.

We fitted him out with his gear and provided funds enough, and made him acquainted too with something of the relations between Jiang and Lin, and between Tao and me. All this goes without saying; and by the time he set off, it was already after the Lantern Festival.

At this juncture, the Chinese Communist “Northeast People’s Liberation Army” was assaulting Anshan and Liaoyang, seeking to seize Yingkou. Lin Biao was there; whether Li Mingqiu had gone I did not know, and what weighed on my mind was whether he could find these two target men.

In the third month, Mr. Zheng Jiemin, inspecting the North China work, reached Beiping. I reported this affair to him from first to last, and he gave instructions. First: to win over Li Mingqiu as far as might be, and not to hold his past against him.
Second: through Li’s connections, to keep up contact with the other side, and, besides fixing the eye upon strategic intelligence, to hope for the raising of the level of the work.
Third, to take special note: in making contact with the other side, the intervention of Luo Ronghuan should be avoided.
Fourth: to go about it with a free hand—the whole responsibility would be his.
According to the actual circumstances, I made my explanation too: that to win over Li Mingqiu was little likely, and that the raising of the level of the work must be as circumstances should allow.

As to the point of avoiding Luo Ronghuan, one could of course not ask much; my own understanding was that Luo was political commissar of the Chinese Communist “Northeast People’s Liberation Army,” his standing in the Party above Lin Biao’s, and several grades higher than Tao Zhu’s. This man was full of resource and stratagem, and must be the number-one chief in charge of the “social department” (special operations) within the Chinese Communist Party. But Li Mingqiu had already gone, and the charge came too late; I could only say that I had noted it.

Li Mingqiu was gone two or three months before he returned to Tianjin, and the news of his return was again “Elder Cousin’s” passing-on to us. I hoped he could come to Beiping, but he had fallen ill again.
He had truly borne every kind of toil and hardship, enduring hunger and cold, before he got to see Lin Biao in a village near Siping.

The words that follow were all told me by Li Mingqiu, brokenly and without head or tail. He said, “Lin Biao’s manner was fairly kindly, though he seemed to have no mind to listen closely to my words.” “Lin Biao urged me again and again to stay and go no more.” “Presently he sent for Tao Zhu, made the introduction, and then Lin left. It was but this one hurried meeting, and there was no concrete word. As Lin departed, he said he would find time to talk it over at length; but afterward I heard he had gone off to some other place.” Li said again, “Tao asked after your circumstances, and seemed much concerned. Tao said to me: ‘Go back and tell him to be quick to win merit for the people—the chances are many, and he must not err again and yet again.’” Li thought a while and told me further, “Tao and I talked more than once; on one occasion he said a thing whose meaning was that before long he would send someone to see you, and would then convey to you their ‘demand.’” Hearing Li Mingqiu tell it to this point, I thought to myself that it had fallen out just as I foresaw; and as to what manner of man might be found to come and meet me, that indeed I must guard against with care.
The general result was just this. The rest was what Li saw and heard along the road, and some “gleanings of talk” from his chatting with Tao Zhu.
In truth, this was the very thing I needed.
I fixed this material fast in my mind, and after handling it with care and adding notes of explanation, reported it to the Corps Headquarters, to be transmitted to the Ministry of National Defense.
The large sum of prize money bestowed by the Ministry of National Defense on the First Brigade, spoken of above, was precisely by reason of the value of this intelligence.

“Value” is a thing of measure and limit, and vanishes with the passing of time. Look, then, once more at the endings and the fates of several of the chief figures in this story. Li Mingqiu, from this illness, never rose again, and some months later died at Tianjin.

Jiang Tian, at the beginning of the thirty-eighth year, did not withdraw with the force but stayed at Beiping. I urged him to go, but he would not listen, being fully persuaded that even when the Communists came they would do him no harm. After the Chinese Communists had usurped the mainland, Lin Biao placed him in a children’s school attached to the Chinese Communist Ministry of Railways, where he served as a warden. Who could have thought that, from the fortieth year on, the “Three-Anti” and “Five-Anti,” and then the “Suppression of Counter-revolutionaries,” would drag him out and shoot him?

Zhang Zuoxing, influenced by Jiang Tian, seemed to have taken it for a support. In the “Suppression of Counter-revolutionaries” he too was dragged out and struggled against again and again, and at the last was sentenced to a “death penalty with reprieve,” removed to the “Chading Farm” near Tangshan for “reform through labor,” where, alas, he perished in the great Tangshan earthquake.

Tao Zhu had for a while his fine hour of glory, of which I have already spoken above. At the time when he was being tormented past all bearing by the “Red Guards” at his residence in Zhongnanhai, it fell out just then that a daughter of his was to be married, and he had not so much as a keepsake to give her, but in the end took off the woolen vest from his own body to serve as her dowry. Not long after, he too died in a “remolding camp” in Anhui.

Lin Biao died in a manner darker and stranger still: it is said that, by an air crash, he died midway on his flight toward Russia, his very corpse burned beyond all recognition. Was it so, or was it not? To this day it remains a riddle. And the writer—I myself? Heaven has sentenced me first to make this “record of the brush,” and to await the “summons.”
